title: Nodal Orbital-Anti-Phase Superconducting State in Bilayer Nickelates
authors: Marius Scholten, Steffen Bötzel, Frank Lechermann, Rafael M. Fernandes, Ilya M. Eremin
abstract: The recent discovery of high-$T_c$ superconductivity in the bilayer nickelate La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ (La-327) under applied pressure and compressive strain opened a new avenue to elucidate the interplay between multiorbital intralayer and interlayer electronically driven Cooper-pairing in bilayer systems. Depending on the details of the electronic structure in the normal state, the superconducting gap in bilayer nickelates is predicted to have either bonding-antibonding $s_{\pm}$-wave symmetry, driven by dominant interlayer Cooper-pairing, or $d$-wave symmetry with substantial intralayer Cooper-pairing. Despite this general picture, the orbital structure of the superconducting gap in these multiorbital systems has been less explored. Here, we analyze the consequences of an orbital-anti-phase structure of the superconducting gap and discuss its possible experimental signatures. We demonstrate that additional pairs of nodes may appear on the $α$ and/or $β$ Fermi surface sheets due to the sign change of the superconducting gap between the involved orbitals. Apart from this additional nodal structure, which is not enforced by the symmetries of the gap function and can be probed in ARPES experiments, the orbital-anti-phase gap modifies the temperature dependence of the superfluid stiffness at low temperatures, providing a concrete experimental prediction to test its realization in bilayer nickelates and related multiorbital systems.
summary: This theoretical work investigates the superconducting gap symmetry in bilayer nickelates, focusing on the unique case of an orbital-anti-phase pairing structure. The authors predict that this specific gap configuration will lead to novel nodal structures on the Fermi surface and will alter the low-temperature behavior of the superfluid stiffness. These predictions offer concrete, testable signatures for experimental verification in related multiorbital superconductors.
main_problem: The paper analyzes the consequences of an orbital-anti-phase structure of the superconducting gap in bilayer nickelates and discusses potential experimental signatures.
main_result: The orbital-anti-phase structure predicts the appearance of additional nodal structures on the Fermi surface sheets and modifies the temperature dependence of the superfluid stiffness at low temperatures.
method: The analysis uses theoretical modeling based on the Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) Hamiltonian, deriving nodal conditions by setting energy eigenvalues to zero.
model_or_system: The system is bilayer nickelates, specifically $	ext{La}_3	ext{Ni}_2	ext{O}_7$, modeled using an effective four-orbital approach that simplifies to a two-orbital bilayer model.
key_observables: Additional nodal structure (probed by ARPES) and the temperature dependence of the superfluid stiffness.
important_parameters: The relative phase shift ($\pi$-shift) between superconducting order parameters on different orbitals, and the parameters characterizing intra- and inter-layer/orbital pairing components.
main_assumptions: The analysis explores the consequences of the orbital-anti-phase gap structure, which is not enforced by symmetry alone.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the normal state Fermi surface topology ($\alpha,  eta, \gamma$ sheets) in bilayer nickelates, showing orbital weights derived from $d_{x^2-y^2}$ and $d_{z^2-r^2}$ orbitals.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the general superconducting gap symmetries to analyzing the specific consequences of the orbital-anti-phase structure, deriving nodal conditions, and finally predicting measurable thermodynamic signatures like the superfluid stiffness modification.
why_interesting: While focused on cuprate/nickelate superconductivity, the detailed theoretical framework involving multi-orbital pairing symmetries, gap structure analysis, and predicting measurable signatures (like nodal changes) is highly relevant to understanding complex pairing mechanisms in strongly correlated electron systems.
